cards.title: Task-centered Approach
cards.textTop: The task-centered approach emphasizes designing instruction around authentic, real-world problems that learners are likely to encounter.
cards.textBottom: An example of applying this practice to a real lesson would be in the drawing of attention to patterns observed in the real world. The repetitious nature of quilts, as seen above, is a natural example of a pattern.
cards.citation: Merrill’s principles of instruction (MPI). Current Students - Tippie College of Business | The University of Iowa. (n.d.).

cards.title: Activation
cards.textTop: The activation principle focuses on engaging learners' prior knowledge and experiences to create a foundation for new learning.
cards.textBottom: Once the lesson is contextualized via the quilt examples, the lesson can be continued by focusing on how patterns can be applied directly in the context of computer science. For example, the lesson can focus on how patterns are used in programming and how they can be applied to solve problems in software development.

cards.title: Demonstration
cards.textTop: The demonstration principle emphasizes providing clear models or examples that illustrate the desired learning outcomes. Learners observe these demonstrations to develop an understanding of how to perform the desired tasks.
cards.textBottom: The example demonstrated would involve the learning of nested loops and how this technique can populate a canvas with minimal lines of code. This lesson would obviously assume the students have a base knowledge of loops and X/Y coordinates beforehand.

cards.title: Application
cards.textTop: The activation principle focuses on engaging learners' prior knowledge and experiences to create a foundation for new learning.
cards.textBottom: In the application phase, students would be asked to emulate the nested loop technique on their own using the scaffolding and examples provided thus far.

cards.title: Integration
cards.textTop: The activation principle focuses on engaging learners' prior knowledge and experiences to create a foundation for new learning.
cards.textBottom: Finally, at the integration phase of the principles, students would be asked to further the nested loop technique by creating their own unique patterns on the canvas using previously practiced shapes and their own knowledge of color theory. This would allow students to demonstrate their understanding of the concept and apply it in a way that is unique to them.
